story_text.value:
I've resuscitated a project I was working on years ago.

I was tired of having nested `flat_map` making my code basically unreadable just to fetch a simple value. The idea is to make simple & readable the traversing of deeply nested structures like JSON responses, while staying in Ruby & keeping its flexibility. Here it goes:

    graphql_response.then(&'[data][repository][issues][edges]*([node][title])')
    # => ["Support negative indexes", "Document aggregates"]

    github_prs_response.then(&'*[draft].any?')
    # => true
It's different from jq or JSONPath in that: - it's a Ruby block so you can use it with `map`, `find`, etc. - you can call Ruby method from it - it doesn't automatically flatten arrays, you decide - it raises on `nil` by default (unless you use `&`, i.e. `[customer][address]&[city]`)

Obviously, it has drawbacks: - it's yet another syntax to learn - it monkey-patches `String` which might be a blocker for some

I'm really looking for feedback here, what do you think? Is it worth releasing a gem with this value proposition?

title.value: Show HN: String#to_proc` to Help Traversing JSON

story_text.value:
I am the founder of Human Assisted Intelligence and I believe AI can be used to reduce polarization and improve the way people communicate and reach agreement.

At https://mediationbench.com/, there are many frontier LLMs tested, but it is difficult to keep up. I've been trying to get more free openrouter or huggingface credits. Azure for OpenAI and Anthropic have both provided token credits. (Thank You!)

The research paper is there as well.

There have been efforts to use LLMs to lie and play diplomacy, which are excellent compliments to this work.

In v4, the test will get harder as Claude nearly saturated the test. Astra was surprisingly low, perhaps because of alignment or safety efforts.

I'd love to get feedback and hear from all of you. I've been working on related ideas for 20 years, so it's definitely a passion project with too much time in isolation.

story_text.value:
I missed a return window last month because the policy page and the order confirmation said different things.
Turns out return windows don't exist as data anywhere. So I've been reading them by hand. 248 shops, 8 countries. Each record stores the sentence the number came from, the URL and the date I read it. 331 more are in the list unread and marked as such.
Free, no signup. MCP server at pricemend.com/mcp if you want an agent to use it.
An early version of my parser read "within one year of the event date" off Target's gift registry page and recorded a 365 day return window. That's why there's a quote on every record now.
Is the confidence field useful, or over-engineered?

story_text.value:
If you already have multiple coding agents(one kind of agent also works though), you should really look into this project! It's a desktop app that brings coding agents working together, with user experience similar to ChatGPT!

One kind of agent is enough for an agent team: all of one kind, or any mix of Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor Agent, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot CLI, Muse Code and five open-source coding agents on your own model backends. For each question, the lead agent designs the team: each member’s role and model, and how they take turns. Once you confirm it, the real agents on your machine work on your code, or any question, and answer each other.

It also supports voice input, notification, branching in conversation, task scheduling, and mobile app(PWA) support!

If you are interested in this project, please give it a try and star us on the GitHub repo, thanks!

GitHub repo: https://github.com/Agentic-System-Lab/harness-relay

story_text.value:
I have trained a custom 31,253 parameter encoder-only transformer on a pregenerated synthetic CGM dataset and fitted it to my own personal data using LoRA. It is competitive among other published models. I used 115 days of CGM data, of which 80 was used for training the adapter and 35 for testing. The model began with a pretraining stage where it consumed ~19,200 CGM-years worth of synthetic data, consisting of 1 million simulated type 1 diabetics at 7 days each. The simulator is designed to aid in counterfactual reasoning, but I don't yet have a benchmark to test these capabilities downstream. Simply using these models on my phone gives me the impression that they do indeed react appropriately when forced to consider future insulin & carbs.

In addition to time series input, two additional inputs are provided: insulin (U) and carbs (G, GI) as action curves where U = units of insulin, G = carbs in grams, GI = glycemic index. U is exact, while (G, GI) is my best estimate.

The model is trained to output BG in Kovatchev risk-space using {DILATE,MSE} and pinball loss combined with learned Kendall-Gal weights. The figures above show models trained using DILATE. It can predict 2 hours into the future, infill missing traces, and do backcasts (predictions into the past).

The model is also trained to predict time-of-day given past blood sugar, in contrast to other models that consume time-of-day as input feature. This capability emerges in >=48h context windows (i.e. 48 hours of past CGM trace). Natively the model has a variable context window size of 3.5 - 7.0 days.

The model is still worse than me when it comes to predicting hypoglycemia in the next ~30 minutes.

story_text.value:
Hi! I just published my first ever mobile game (and mobile app altogether). It consists in a "campaign" of 20 Tic Tac Toe variants, from basic ones (the first level is literally just Tic Tac Toe) to some way more complex and cool.

The rules of the variants are not explained through the campaign so you have to play and guess as you go, I tried to make each new level surprising in its own way :)

The idea came to me because along the years I've seen a surprising number of Tic Tac Toe custom rules and thought it would be cool to make a whole game out of it. I settled on 20 levels but have a ton more ideas and I'll probably add some in later updates.

Surprisingly to me the hardest part was publishing an app on the App Store and Play Store (still pending because it requires 12 testers), the whole process was pretty nightmarish. At least I had a lot of fun making the game itself!

story_text.value:
Site URL: https://fmrl.live

Repository URL: https://gitlab.com/croatoa/fmrl

This project allows you to host a website, content, and streaming from an open browser window. It gets served over WebRTC connections (or a Cloudfare turn server if that's not available).

This is just a start. Any suggestions or feedback to improve usability, feature requests, etc is super welcome.

This is a project I've had in mind for a while. I wanted to participate in building for a decentralized web, so I thought it would be cool if people could run a social network kind of page from their own machine, and allow them to diffuse content over a peer to peer net, independent of the typical social media giants.

While this iteration is not quite that, it's a start.

While the UI probably makes this super obvious, this is the first time I've used AI in coding (LLM, Claude Code). It really is some impressive machinery.

The goal isn't privacy, but rather autonomy, more or less. I know there are real limitations (like a host user closing their browser) but I feel like the idea is at least slightly novel (probably because its a mediocre idea lol).. but it'll be interesting to see how it evolves.

If you made it this far, thanks for the read. Hope you have a pleasant day.

title.value: Show HN: Host a site, content, or stream from a browser tab, served over WebRTC

story_text.value:
Hi folks

I've started this project years ago as an "exercise" and it stalled completely very soon, for years due to various reasons. But recently i've decided that it was worth a shot to actually make something useful out of it and show to the world. Yep, the world that's already full of link shorteners\link management software\branded links services\etc.

I realise that there's a lot of established options in this space and I clearly realise that there's no "moat" in software like this nowadays, but it feels really great to see not yet another tombstone in my graveyard of started-and-never-finished projects, but a publicly available tool, that can be used by people.

While working on it, i've realised that a "link shortener" nowadays is much more than fitting a long link in a message or whatever. It can actually be a fun tool to o̶v̶e̶r̶-̶e̶n̶g̶i̶n̶e̶e̶r̶ build, while you're exploring all the areas it can be used in.

If you'll find it useful for your project/job - I'd be happy to hear your thoughts on any aspect of it, let me know.
